learningObjectives.title: Wealth, poverty and the responsibilities of wealth
Social justice, charity and exploitation of the poor

questions.q: According to Genesis 1:27, human beings are made 'in the image of God'. What is this belief often used to argue?
options: That every human has equal, God-given value and dignity
That only Christians have human rights
That humans are superior to God
That the body is unimportant
questions.explain: The idea of the imago Dei is used to argue that all people share equal worth and should be treated with dignity.

questions.q: In which year was the Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted by the United Nations?
questions.explain: The UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948, setting out rights and freedoms for all people.

questions.q: What is the key difference between prejudice and discrimination?
options: Prejudice is unfair pre-judgement in the mind, while discrimination is acting on it
Prejudice is always legal but discrimination never is
They mean exactly the same thing
Prejudice is a physical action and discrimination is only a thought
questions.explain: Prejudice is holding biased opinions about someone, whereas discrimination is putting that prejudice into action.

questions.q: The Parable of the Good Samaritan is most often used by Christians to teach what?
options: That people should love and help their neighbour regardless of background
That only priests deserve help
That wealth should never be shared
That travellers should avoid strangers
questions.explain: The Samaritan helps a stranger of a different group, teaching that neighbourly love crosses social and ethnic boundaries.

questions.q: What is meant by 'positive discrimination'?
options: Treating a disadvantaged group more favourably to correct past inequality
Refusing to employ people because of their religion
Ignoring people's rights entirely
Punishing a group for its beliefs
questions.explain: Positive discrimination means giving preferential treatment to a group that has faced disadvantage, and it is a debated approach.

questions.q: An employer refuses to interview an applicant purely because of the applicant's religion. This is best described as an example of:
options: Religious discrimination
Freedom of religious expression
Positive discrimination
Social justice
questions.explain: Acting unfairly against someone because of their religious beliefs is religious discrimination.

questions.q: The Bible teaching '(the) love of money is a root of all kinds of evil' comes from which book?
options: 1 Timothy
Genesis
Exodus
Revelation
questions.explain: This teaching is found in 1 Timothy 6:10 and warns against greed rather than money itself.

questions.q: Jesus said it is 'easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God'. What does this teach?
options: That attachment to wealth can be a barrier to a right relationship with God
That all rich people go to hell
That money should be destroyed
That poverty is a sin
questions.explain: The saying warns that clinging to riches can distract people from God and spiritual priorities.

questions.q: Many religious believers teach that wealth carries responsibilities. What is a common example of such a responsibility?
options: Using wealth to help those in need
Hoarding wealth for its own sake
Refusing to work
Spending only on oneself
questions.explain: Both Christianity and Islam teach that wealth should be used generously to support the poor and vulnerable.

questions.q: Why do some Christians view wealth positively rather than as inherently sinful?
options: Because wealth can be a blessing used responsibly as a steward of God's gifts
Because money proves a person is holy
Because the poor deserve their poverty
Because giving to charity is forbidden
questions.explain: Many Christians see wealth as morally neutral, becoming good or bad depending on how it is used and shared.

questions.q: A wealthy Muslim businessman decides how to handle his savings for the year. Which action reflects the Islamic idea of the responsibilities of wealth?
options: Giving a set portion of his surplus wealth to those in need
Charging the poor high interest on loans
Keeping all his wealth hidden and unused
Ignoring the needs of the ummah
questions.explain: Islam teaches that wealth is a trust from Allah and that a portion should be shared with the needy, as in zakah.

questions.q: Zakah, one of the Five Pillars of Islam, usually requires Muslims to give what proportion of their surplus wealth each year?
questions.explain: Zakah is normally calculated as 2.5% of a Muslim's surplus savings and wealth given annually to the poor.

questions.q: What is 'sadaqah' in Islam?
options: Voluntary charity given out of kindness
A compulsory tax of 2.5%
A forbidden form of interest
A pilgrimage to Makkah
questions.explain: Sadaqah is voluntary giving, additional to the obligatory zakah, motivated by generosity and compassion.

questions.q: What is meant by 'social justice'?
options: Ensuring society is fair and that everyone has equal rights and opportunities
Making sure the wealthy keep all their money
Punishing the poor for being poor
Removing all laws from society
questions.explain: Social justice is concerned with fairness and equal treatment for all members of society, especially the disadvantaged.

questions.q: In Islam, what is 'riba'?
options: Charging interest on loans, which is forbidden
Voluntary charity
A form of prayer
A festival of giving
questions.explain: Riba refers to charging interest, which Islam prohibits because it is seen as exploiting those in need.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of the exploitation of the poor?
options: Paying workers unfairly low wages while making large profits
Giving generously to a food bank
Providing fair-trade goods
Offering interest-free loans to the needy
questions.explain: Exploitation involves treating people unfairly for personal gain, such as underpaying vulnerable workers.

questions.q: Which of the following is a Christian charity that works to relieve poverty?
options: Christian Aid
The Five Pillars
Zakah Foundation of Prayer
The Golden Temple Trust
questions.explain: Christian Aid, along with CAFOD and Tearfund, is a Christian organisation that tackles poverty and injustice.

questions.q: In the Parable of the Sheep and the Goats (Matthew 25), what does Jesus teach about helping the poor and needy?
options: That whatever is done for the needy is done for Jesus himself
That the poor should be ignored
That charity is a waste of time
That only wealthy people will be saved
questions.explain: The parable teaches that caring for the hungry, sick and imprisoned is treated as serving Christ himself.

questions.q: A lender offers loans to poor families at extremely high interest rates they can barely repay. A Muslim would most likely condemn this as an example of:
options: Riba and exploitation of the poor
Zakah and social justice
Sadaqah and charity
Fair and just business
questions.explain: Charging excessive interest to the vulnerable is riba and is seen as exploiting those in need.

questions.q: A Christian joins a peaceful campaign against racist laws, arguing all people are equal before God. This best reflects which principle?
options: Standing up for human rights and against discrimination
Supporting the exploitation of the poor
Encouraging prejudice
Rejecting social justice
questions.explain: Peacefully opposing unjust, discriminatory laws is an example of defending human rights, as seen in figures like Martin Luther King.

specSource: AQA GCSE Religious Studies A specification; Theme F: Religion, Human Rights & Social Justice
